text.p: Transport group Scott Corp Ltd is planning to improve net profit in 1996/97 in a still tough industry environment, new managing director Ivan Backman said on Tuesday.
"Yes, I believe we will have an improved net profit (on 1995/96's A$5.2 million)," Backman told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Asked if the transport industry, strongly exposed to a slower economy, could expect substantial earnings growth beyond 1996/97, he said: "It is tight, there is no doubt about that."
"I would see next year as still being reasonably tight, but I look forward to the one after that as being an improved scenario," he said.

Backman said 1996/97 improvement for Scott Corp would come through the A$40 million per year Smorgon steel contract, rationalisation of the Blakistons business, efficiencies from two new terminals, and an extremely good performance from K&S Express which "will be one of our winners this year".
The final accounts would show some abnormals relating to the final rationalisation of Blakistons which "will have some impact but not, I hope, a huge one (on the bottom line)," he said.
Backman, who joined Scott Corp in July after 18 years with the privately owned Linfox Transport, said development of the company's logistics business was the main focus for the future.

"If we are not involved in that, our business will stagnate and go backwards: the demand from our existing client base is such that they want the 'one-stop shop' scenario, so I believe it will rather enhance our ability to make profits," he said.
"The line haul work will always be tough and tight but adding value should give us ability to add some additional margin - but if we do not add value we will not get the work."
He said it was difficult to quantify logistics growth from its current 20 percent share of company earnings, because the concept would ultimately become intrinsic to total operations.

Backman said Scott Corp would pursue growth through its existing client base and aggressive pursuit of new clients, moving also to broaden its current reliance on the cyclical building sector into other areas such as food transport.

Strategic acquisition was also a clear opportunity as rationalisation, which has seen former transport giants TNT Ltd, Brambles Industries Ltd and Mayne Nickless Ltd exit the sector, continued, he said.
"I see further rationalisation, even in the middle sized distribution people, so that will cause availability of specific people we would want to be in bed with, take over," he said.

He did not rule out interest in some of TNT's freight operations, which the big transport company announced in July it would offload, and said acqusition was likely to be aligned more to providing services in Scott's logistics chain than line haul.
He could also see opportunities for growth in the longer-term in south-east Asia, and in the opening up to private operators of Australia's national rail freight network, he said.
"(Rail) is one of the opportunities in the future and that is where there might be room for amalgamation of people who are large volume movers," he said.

Backman said alliances, mergers and takeovers involving the newly emerged major transporters - Scott, Finemore Holdings Ltd, Toll Holdings Ltd, and Linfox - also were possible in the long-term but there was still room for them all now.
"I think there is room for that sort of merger...in the future but not immediately necessarily," he said.

He played down any imminent prospects, amid continuing market speculation, for a merger between Scott Corp and its chairman and major stakeholder Alan Scott's private operation Scott Transport Industries.

"Whilst there are synergies, I think Alan is very happy to keep his own business, and I am very comfortable with him keeping that....it is a future possibility but it has been a future possibility for some time now," he said.
